subtype: Approach: mixing practice with fun to stay motivated [Revision]
passage: Ayaan's fingers knew the C major scale so well that his mind drifted to the window by the third round. On Thursday, at keyboard class in their housing society hall, he finally asked, "Ma'am, can we learn the tune from that new film? The one everyone hums?" Lalremsiami smiled and pencilled the first line into his notebook. "Scales and the two exercises first," she said. "Then the tune is yours." That evening Ayaan played the scales twice, slow and clean, and then slid into the song, humming under his breath. By the weekend a note was stuck on the keyboard lid: exercises first, song second.

qa.q: What did Ayaan play after finishing his scales and exercises each day?
qa.a: After the scales and exercises, Ayaan played the song from the new film.

qa.q: What was Ayaan feeling during the third round of the scale, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was bored, because his mind drifted to the window even though his fingers already knew the notes. 🥱

qa.q: What other approach could help Ayaan stay interested in practice, and why might it work?
qa.a: He could split practice into short timed parts with a small target for each, since a clear goal keeps the mind from wandering.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami see Ayaan's request?
qa.a: Lalremsiami probably sees it as a sign that Ayaan wants to keep learning, since she smiled and wrote out the song while keeping the exercises first.

grounding: A boy bored by scales asks for a film tune and uses it as a daily reward after his exercises.

subtype: Approach: ignoring the teasing at first [Thinking]
passage: If I say nothing, Kasper will get bored, Omar told himself on the walk to school in Rotterdam. Nobody wants to be boring, not even a bully. On Monday Kasper flicked his ear and called him "Sleepy Omar". Omar kept his eyes on his sums and said nothing. On Tuesday Kasper gave up after two tries and went back to his lunch. Omar felt lighter, almost proud. But by Friday the nickname had reached two other boys, and Kasper was back, louder, waiting at the gate. Omar's stomach tightened. Maybe saying nothing was only the first step, he thought, and not the whole plan.

qa.q: What nickname did Kasper give Omar?
qa.a: Kasper called him "Sleepy Omar".

qa.q: What was Omar feeling on Friday when Kasper was waiting at the gate?
qa.a: Worried, because his stomach tightened as he realised that saying nothing was not enough on its own.

qa.q: What other approach could Omar add to ignoring, and why?
qa.a: He could tell a teacher what has been happening, because the nickname is spreading and an adult can act where silence alone cannot.

qa.q: How might Kasper have read Omar's silence on Monday and Tuesday?
qa.a: At first it may have felt dull, which fits Kasper giving up after two tries, but later Kasper may have taken the silence as a sign that Omar would not answer back.

grounding: A boy hopes ignoring the bully will make him lose interest; it helps briefly but the teasing continues.

subtype: Approach: telling a teacher or parent with details [Action]
passage: My name is Jasleen, and this is about the term I stopped saying "somebody keeps bothering me" and started saying exactly what happened. In my rough notebook I wrote: Tuesday, before assembly, Dev called my plait a rope and said I smelled of onions. Wednesday, at the water tap, the same again. Heard by Meher and Iqbal. I wrote it small, with the days. Then I took the page to our class teacher, Mrs Vandana, at recess. She read it twice, asked me two questions, and said it helped because now she knew what to check and whom to ask. The next day she spoke to Dev, and my shoulders came down a little.

qa.q: Which two classmates did Jasleen list as having heard Dev's remarks?
qa.a: Meher and Iqbal heard what Dev said.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel after handing the page to Mrs Vandana?
qa.a: Relieved, because Jasleen's shoulders came down once the facts were with the teacher. 😊

qa.q: What could Jasleen do if the remarks continued after the talk with Dev?
qa.a: Keep adding dated notes and share them with a parent as well, because a record of repeated events helps adults decide what to do.

qa.q: Why did the written page make Mrs Vandana's job easier?
qa.a: She could see what was said, on which days and who had heard it, so she knew what to check instead of guessing.

grounding: Jasleen records what was said, when and who saw it, and gives it to the class teacher.

passage: I sit two rows behind Sumit, so I saw most of it. For weeks Manoj had been taking Sumit's pencil case and laughing when Sumit reached for it. At recess on Thursday Manoj did it again, and Sumit shoved him hard against the railing with both hands. Manoj fell and yelled, and then the teacher on duty was there. Sumit's face was red and his eyes looked wet, though I can't say if that was anger or fear. Both boys were marched to the principal's office. Sumit came back with a note in his diary for home. I'm Nisha, by the way, and I wish I had said something sooner.

qa.q: What did Sumit do to Manoj at recess on Thursday?
qa.a: Sumit shoved Manoj hard against the railing with both hands.

qa.q: What might Sumit have been feeling when the teacher on duty arrived?
qa.a: Probably angry and frightened at once, since his face was red and his eyes looked wet, though Nisha admits it is hard to be sure.

qa.q: What approach could Sumit have used instead of pushing, and why?
qa.a: He could have told the teacher about the pencil case being taken, because the taking would be dealt with and Sumit would not end up in trouble too.

qa.q: How might Manoj have seen the push?
qa.a: Manoj may have been shocked and hurt, and for that day it turned the bully into the one who was pushed, which is the opposite of what Sumit wanted.

grounding: A boy pushes the bully at recess and both are sent to the principal, so revenge leaves him in trouble too.

subtype: Approach: staying with a group of friends [Action]
passage: Tuesday, 8 pm. Figured something out. Harish only bothers me when I'm on my own, by the lockers or at the bus stop before anyone comes. When my friend Tara was standing next to me last week, he just walked past. So today I tried it. Tara and Meena, my two friends, both said yes, and we walked to the bus together. At break I sat on the bench beside Mr Rao's table. Harish looked over twice and then went off to the far wall. No name-calling at all! Not a fix forever, I know, but my tummy feels less knotted tonight. Tomorrow I'll do the same again. Sabina

qa.q: Who did Sabina walk to the bus with?
qa.a: Sabina walked to the bus with Tara and Meena.

qa.q: How does Sabina feel at the end of the entry, and what shows it?
qa.a: Cautiously relieved: Sabina's tummy feels less knotted, though Sabina knows it is not a fix forever. 🙂

qa.q: What else could Sabina do if Harish started bothering Sabina when the friends are not around?
qa.a: Tell a teacher or a parent what happened, with details, because a group only helps while it is there and adults can change what happens in the gaps.

qa.q: How does the plan look from Tara's side?
qa.a: Tara said yes straight away, so Tara seems to see it as a simple way to help and to spend time together.

grounding: Sabina sees the bully picks only on someone alone, so Sabina walks with two friends and sits near the teacher at break.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing a calm firm reply [Thinking]
passage: Vishal waited until his sister left for the well, then stood in front of the small mirror in the kitchen. "Stop it," he said. Too squeaky. He tried again, lower and slower: "Stop it." Then he turned and took three steps, as if leaving the school gate. He pictured Ritu laughing, maybe copying his voice. "Then I keep walking," he whispered. "Laughing is only noise." He did it ten times, until the words came out steady and his hands stopped shaking. Next morning at the hand pump Ritu began the usual jokes. Vishal's voice was thin, but it held, and he walked away without looking back.

qa.q: Where did Vishal practise saying "Stop it"?
qa.a: He practised in front of the small mirror in the kitchen.

qa.q: Why did Vishal picture Ritu laughing before it happened?
qa.a: He was nervous and wanted to feel steady, so he imagined the laugh and decided in advance that it was only noise.

qa.q: What could Vishal add to his plan if Ritu keeps teasing after he walks away?
qa.a: He could tell a teacher what was said and when, because a calm reply may not be enough by itself and an adult can step in.

qa.q: How might a steady "Stop it" feel to Ritu compared with a squeaky one?
qa.a: A steady voice gives Ritu less to laugh at, so Ritu may lose interest, while a shaky voice could feel like a reward for teasing.

grounding: A boy rehearses a calm firm reply and walking away, imagining the bully's reaction so he is steadier.

subtype: Approach: trying to become friends with the bully [Thinking]
passage: Wednesday night. Irfan called my glasses "bottle bottoms" again today. I nearly cried, but then I noticed something: nobody sits with Irfan at lunch, ever. Maybe that's why. Maybe lonely people get mean. First thing in the morning I told Ms Dsouza, because Amma says grown-ups must know. She wrote it down. Then at lunch I said, "Nice drawing," about the dinosaur on Irfan's folder. Irfan blinked and said "thanks", and said nothing mean all lunch! But at the bus stop it started again. So a kind word isn't magic. Telling Ms Dsouza matters more. Tomorrow I'll tell her about the bus too. Trisha

qa.q: What did Trisha say to Irfan at lunch?
qa.a: Trisha said "Nice drawing" about the dinosaur on Irfan's folder.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when Irfan mocked the glasses, and what changed the thought?
qa.a: Trisha felt hurt and nearly cried, but noticing that nobody sits with Irfan made Trisha wonder whether loneliness was behind the teasing.

qa.q: What should Trisha do besides trying kind words, and why?
qa.a: Keep telling Ms Dsouza, including about the bus, since the kind word only worked sometimes and an adult can deal with the teasing itself.

qa.q: What might lunch be like for Irfan?
qa.a: Lonely, because nobody sits with Irfan, so a kind comment about the folder may have been a rare friendly moment, which fits the surprised blink and the "thanks".

grounding: Trisha wonders if the bully is lonely, tells a teacher, and also tries a kind word, seeing it is not a substitute for adult help.

subtype: Approach: hiding at home and skipping school [Pitfall]
passage: Come, sit, Meera. Let me tell you about my own stomach aches. I am Hemant, and when I was a boy of ten, another boy named Dinesh waited by the school gate every morning to snatch my cap. So I began groaning at breakfast. "My head, Aai, my stomach." Three days at home, warm blanket, no Dinesh. Lovely! By the fourth day the relief was gone and a heavy feeling had taken its place, because Monday was still coming. That evening my mother sat on my bed and said, "You are not really ill, are you? What is wrong?" Out it all came. She did not scold. She held my hand and said we would tell the teacher together.

qa.q: What did Dinesh do to Hemant every morning at the school gate?
qa.a: Dinesh waited at the school gate to snatch Hemant's cap.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling on the fourth day at home?
qa.a: A heavy worry, because the relief had gone and Monday, and Dinesh, was still coming.

qa.q: What could Hemant have done instead of pretending to be ill, and why?
qa.a: He could have told his mother or a teacher on the first day, because adults could then deal with Dinesh and Hemant would not lose days of school.

qa.q: How might Hemant's mother have felt when he finally told her?
qa.a: Probably concerned, and glad that he trusted her, since she asked gently, did not scold and held his hand.

grounding: A boy fakes illness to avoid the bully, which gives short relief until his mother notices and asks what is wrong.

subtype: Approach: changing the plan when the first step fails [Revision]
passage: For two weeks Sharmila had kept her eyes on her notebook while Tanmay and his two friends whispered "Chashmish" behind her in class. Ignoring it was supposed to work. Instead the whispers got louder, and on Friday her pencil box went missing. That evening Sharmila sat on her bed and counted: two weeks, no change. New plan. She told her parents everything, in order. Her father listened, her mother wrote down the dates, and on Monday both went to see the class teacher. By Wednesday the seating had been rearranged, Tanmay's group sat near the front, and the teacher's eyes kept passing over that corner. Sharmila still felt shaky, but the whispers had gone quiet.

qa.q: What changed at school after Sharmila's parents met the teacher?
qa.a: The seating was rearranged, and the teacher's eyes kept passing over the corner where Tanmay's group sat.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when she counted the days on her bed?
qa.a: Frustrated and worn down, because two weeks of ignoring had brought no change and she decided she needed a new plan.

qa.q: What could Sharmila do if the whispering started again in the corridor?
qa.a: Tell her class teacher or her parents straight away with the details, because they already know the situation and can extend the watching.

qa.q: How might Sharmila's parents have felt when she told them everything?
qa.a: Probably worried, but glad she told them, since they listened, wrote down the dates and both went to school on Monday.

grounding: A girl finds ignoring the teasing fails, tells her parents, and the school acts by moving seats and watching the group.

subtype: Approach: standing up for a friend with others [Action]
passage: The back-bench boys had started copying the way Jatin read aloud, slow and careful, and on Tuesday at lunch Chetan could not watch any more. On his own he would have stared at his shoes; he knew that. So he nudged Asad and Kabir, and the three of them walked across the classroom and stood beside Jatin's desk. "That isn't funny," Asad said. Nobody laughed. The mockers drifted off. After lunch Chetan went to the class teacher with the other two and told her what they had seen. His knees still wobbled, but standing three in a row had made it possible. Jatin only said "thanks", with his ears pink.

qa.q: Who went with Chetan to stand beside Jatin's desk?
qa.a: Asad and Kabir went with Chetan.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling as he stood beside Jatin?
qa.a: Nervous, since his knees still wobbled, but having two others next to him gave him courage. 😅

qa.q: What other approach could Chetan use if the mocking returned when no one else is near?
qa.a: He could go straight to the class teacher or invite Jatin to sit with another group, because an adult or a crowd can change the situation when he is alone.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel when the three boys stood beside his desk?
qa.a: Probably relieved and a little shy, since his ears turned pink and all Jatin said was thanks.

grounding: A boy goes with two others to stand beside Jatin, who is being mocked, and tells the teacher, finding courage in numbers.
